title: Marketplace Flipping
subtitle: Turn local finds into real value, without letting urgency, mystery links or a suspiciously silent blender run the meeting

blocks.text: A marketplace bargain can be a profitable flip. It can also be a lamp that flickers, a bicycle with an adventurous serial number or an e-transfer screenshot showing the confidence of a theatre major. The inspection comes before the celebration.

Marketplace flipping means buying a used item below its value, fixing it up or presenting it honestly and reselling it locally. Your edge comes from knowing the product and buying with discipline, not pressuring strangers. Every deal needs four kinds of proof: the item is legit, its condition is tested, your profit survives every cost and the payment is real.
Specialize before you grow. Knowing one category’s normal wear, parts, serial number spots and resale range protects you better than being generally hopeful about everything with a plug.

items.title: “Fast replies win the best marketplace deals.”
items.text: Fast replies may win attention. Profitable deals still need inspection, identity checks and payment checks. Urgency is not proof.

blocks.text: CAFC: Merchandise scams
A few checks before every deal protect your money, your safety and your profit.
blocks.detail: Proof that an item is legit, tested, worth the price and paid for turns a lucky find into a business.
blocks.extra: Section 02 shows how to make an item prove its story.

sections.title: Make the Item Prove Its Story

blocks.text: An item earns your money by passing inspection, not by telling a good story.

items.title: RESEARCH THE RANGE
items.text: Compare local sold prices for the exact model and condition. Allow for the season, missing parts and how far a buyer must travel.

items.title: ASK BEFORE YOU DRIVE
items.text: Ask for current photos, the model number, known defects, repair history, what is included and why they are selling. A clear answer saves kilometres and awkward driveway archaeology.

items.title: INSPECT IN PERSON
items.text: Use a checklist for the category. Turn electronics on, test the controls, check for smells and water damage, look at frames and bolts, and make sure promised parts are there.

items.title: CHECK IT IS LEGIT
items.text: Ask for a receipt or reasonable proof of ownership for higher-risk goods. Note serial numbers where allowed, search recalls, and walk away from removed serial numbers, signs of fakes or stories that do not add up.

blocks.text: Search Health Canada’s recall database by brand and model. An item that looks repaired still needs its recall status checked.
For bikes, electronics and other items that get stolen, a missing or altered serial number is a stop sign, not an invitation to improve your negotiating voice.

items.title: “A cosmetic clean-up can make any item ready to resell.”
items.text: Cleaning improves how an item looks. It does not fix electrical faults, cancel a recall or prove ownership. Disclose any remaining defects honestly.

blocks.text: Health Canada: Buying second-hand products

sections.title: Set the Deal Rules Before the Parking Lot

blocks.text: Set your maximum buy price before the meeting. Start with a cautious resale price, then subtract cleaning, parts, travel, selling costs, a risk allowance and your target profit. Bring that number with you.

items.title: Negotiate inside your number
items.text: Offer below your maximum, and walk away if the seller will not meet it. Your number protects you from parking lot pressure.

items.title: Meet somewhere safe
items.text: Meet in daylight in a busy public place. Many police stations have a marked area for online sales. Tell someone where you are going.

items.title: Verify payment yourself
items.text: Open your own banking app and confirm the money is there before you hand over the item. Never trust a screenshot, email or link.

items.title: Record the deal
items.text: Write down what you paid, what you spent fixing it up, what you sold it for and the date. Those records are your profit and your tax proof.

blocks.text: A fake e-transfer message may lead to a fake page that asks for your banking login. Open your bank yourself and check for the deposit there.
Overpayment is a warning sign. A buyer who sends “too much” and asks for a refund may be trying to turn a fake payment into your real money.

items.title: “Cash is always the safest local payment method.”
items.text: Every method has risks. Cash can be fake, and carrying it affects your safety. Follow your platform’s and bank’s advice, meet safely and check the payment yourself.

blocks.text: Selling your own used things, like an old couch or last year’s skates, is generally not taxable, especially when you sell for less than you paid. Buying items so you can sell them for a profit is a business, and that profit is taxable income. Some online marketplaces now also report seller names and sales totals to the CRA each year, unless you made fewer than 30 sales totalling $2,800 or less on that platform.
Tax basics for your first year

items.title: REPORT IT
items.text: Business income goes on Form T2125 with your personal tax return, whether clients pay by cash, cheque or e-transfer.

items.title: PAY BOTH HALVES OF CPP
items.text: Self-employed people pay the worker and employer shares of CPP, 11.9% of net business income above the basic amount, on Schedule 8 of the return.

items.title: SET MONEY ASIDE
items.text: Nobody takes tax off your pay. Move a share of every payment into a separate account. If you owe more than $3,000 ($1,800 in Quebec) this year and in either of the last two years, the CRA will ask for quarterly instalments.

items.title: KEEP RECORDS SIX YEARS
items.text: Keep invoices, receipts, mileage and bank records for six years from the end of the tax year they belong to.

blocks.text: Key takeaway: a flip is only profitable when the item is legit, safe and tested, your maximum buy price protects your margin and you check the payment yourself. A deal you safely turn down can be excellent business.

sections.title: Mateo Checks the Account, Not the Applause

blocks.text: Meet Mateo
paragraphs: Mateo Alvarez flips used camera gear in Calgary. His goal is to save $2,000 for a better camera of his own by summer. He cleans and tests a used lens, and lists it with clear photos of one small scratch.
Four minutes later, a buyer offers full price. Mateo briefly feels like the Warren Buffett of camera lenses.

They meet at a coffee shop. The buyer shows an e-transfer confirmation on his phone. Then he says Mateo needs to click an email link to “upgrade” his account first. The email also asks for a one-time code from his bank. The lens is real. The payment is performing community theatre.
The buyer is friendly and in a hurry. Saying no feels awkward. Mateo decides to check his own banking app before anything else. No deposit is there.
He refuses the link, never shares the code and ends the meeting. Then he reports the account to the platform.
Two days later, a second buyer tests the lens, pays by e-transfer and waits while Mateo checks his own account. The money is there.
The second sale earns a smaller burst of excitement and a real profit. Mateo writes down what he paid, his cleaning supplies, the sale price and the date. Quiet checking beats dramatic screenshots.

blocks.text: Never share a security code your bank sends you. It is meant to approve a login or a payment, not to help a buyer release money.
What resolved the conflict?
The applause for a fast sale was not proof of payment. Only his own bank account was.
Mateo kept his lens and his bank account safe by checking his own app instead of the buyer’s screen.
blocks.detail: The same habit protects every flip you make, no matter how friendly the buyer seems.
blocks.extra: The quick check in Section 05 tests whether you can spot the next move.

sections.title: Quick Check: Choose the Best Next Move

items.title: Why set your maximum buy price before the meeting?
items.detail: Pressure in person can make you overpay. A number set ahead of time protects your profit.

items.title: What should your inspection confirm?
items.detail: That the item works, and that its parts, condition and accessories match what was described, using a checklist for the category.

items.title: How should you check an e-transfer?
items.detail: Look for the deposit in your own banking app. Never trust an email, text, screenshot, QR code or the buyer’s phone screen.

items.title: Which payment requests should end a deal?
items.detail: A request to pay an upgrade fee, refund an overpayment, share a one-time security code or open a courier or payment link from a stranger.

items.title: What must an honest resale listing include?
items.detail: The current condition, any known defects and all required charges, with no misleading prices or fake urgency.

sections.title: Your Action (Fill Out Form): Local Flip Safety Card

blocks.text: Fill this in before you arrange a meeting. Do not write banking passwords, one-time codes, a stranger’s ID or a private home address here.
Use a written walk-away rule. No serial number where there should be one, no safe way to test, a changed meeting place, pressure, overpayment or a request for a login or code means the deal stops.

items.title: Marketplace flip
items.text: A used item you buy to fix up, present well and resell for profit.

items.title: Maximum buy price
items.text: The most you can pay and still cover costs and your target profit.

items.title: Comparable
items.text: A similar item you use to estimate a realistic selling price.

items.title: Serial number
items.text: A unique number on many manufactured products.

items.title: Phishing
items.text: A message or website made to steal your login or financial information.

items.title: Overpayment scam
items.text: A fake or reversible extra payment, followed by a request for a real refund.

items.title: Walk-away rule
items.text: A condition, written ahead of time, that ends a deal.
